about: English meaning written for this library (en-scriptures): one to three plain sentences per mantra, faithful to the Sanskrit, following the traditional reading (Śaṅkara's bhāṣya). [meaning, [footnotes]]; footnotes give brief context and other readings.

m.shanti.1: Om. O gods, may we hear with our ears what is good; O you who are worthy of worship, may we see with our eyes what is good. With steady limbs and bodies, praising you, may we live out the span of life the gods have set. May Indra of great fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, who knows all, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheel no one can harm, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being. Om, peace, peace, peace.
m.m01: Hariḥ Om. Om, this syllable, is all this. Here is its clear explanation: what was, what is and what will be, all is Om alone; and whatever else lies beyond the three times, that too is Om alone.
m.m02: All this is indeed Brahman. This Self is Brahman. This Self has four quarters.
m.m03: The first quarter is Vaiśvānara: its sphere is waking, its awareness turned outward; it has seven limbs and nineteen mouths and enjoys gross things.
m.m04: The second quarter is Taijasa: its sphere is dream, its awareness turned inward; it has seven limbs and nineteen mouths and enjoys subtle things.
m.m05: Where the sleeper desires nothing and sees no dream, that is deep sleep. The third quarter is Prājña: its sphere is deep sleep; in it all has become one; it is a mass of awareness alone, made of bliss, enjoying bliss, and consciousness is its door.
m.m06: This is the Lord of all; this is the knower of all; this is the inner controller; this is the source of all, for from it beings arise and into it they dissolve.
m.m07: Not aware of the inner, not aware of the outer, not aware of both; not a mass of awareness, not knowing, not unknowing; unseen, beyond all dealings, beyond grasp, without marks, beyond thought, beyond words; its essence is the one awareness of the Self; in it the world comes to rest; peaceful, auspicious, without a second: this is thought to be the Fourth. That is the Self; that is to be known.
m.m08: This same Self, seen as a syllable, is Om; seen as its sounds, the quarters are the sounds and the sounds are the quarters: A, U and M.
m.m09: Vaiśvānara, whose sphere is waking, is A, the first sound, because it pervades and because it comes first. Whoever knows this attains all desires and becomes the first.
m.m10: Taijasa, whose sphere is dream, is U, the second sound, because it is higher and because it stands between the two. Whoever knows this raises the flow of knowledge and becomes equal to all; in his family no one is born who does not know Brahman.
m.m11: Prājña, whose sphere is deep sleep, is M, the third sound, because it measures and because all merges into it. Whoever knows this measures all this and becomes that into which all merges.
m.m12: The Fourth has no sound: beyond all dealings, the world at rest in it, auspicious, without a second. So Om is the Self itself. Whoever knows this enters the Self by the Self.

shanti.1: The śānti pāṭha of the Upaniṣads of the Atharvaveda (Praśna, Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya), from the Ṛgveda (1.89.8 and 1.89.6). Tārkṣya is Garuḍa; ariṣṭanemi, “whose wheel-rim is unharmed”, is also read “who wards off harm”. Peace is said three times, for freedom from the troubles that come from oneself, from other beings and from the powers of nature.
m01: Hariḥ Om is the invocation with which the recitation begins. Śaṅkara: the name (Om) and the named (Brahman) are one, and everything is known through its name, so everything is Om.
m02: Ayam ātmā brahma (“this Self is Brahman”) is one of the four great sayings (mahāvākya). The quarters are not like a cow's four feet but like the quarters of a coin: each is understood by merging the one before into it (Śaṅkara).
m03: Seven limbs: heaven as the head, the sun as the eye, air as the breath, space as the trunk, water as the bladder, the earth as the feet and the sacrificial fire as the mouth (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18). Nineteen mouths: the five senses, the five organs of action, the five vital breaths, and mind, intellect, ego and memory (citta).
m04: Taijasa, “the shining one”: in dream the mind itself, made of the impressions of waking, is both the light and the things seen.
m05: As night's darkness covers everything, deep sleep gathers all experience into one undivided awareness, without knower and known. Cetomukha: consciousness is the “mouth” or door through which it goes out again into dream and waking (Śaṅkara).
m06: Said of Prājña: the Self of deep sleep, seen as the cause of everything, is Īśvara, the Lord.
m07: The Fourth (turīya) is not a fourth state beside the other three, but the Self in which all three appear; it can be pointed to only by denying them (Śaṅkara).
m08: Om is analysed as a-u-m, three “measures” (mātrā), matched with the three quarters.
m09: A pervades all speech, as Vaiśvānara pervades the waking world, and A comes first, as waking does.
m10: U stands between A and M as dream stands between waking and sleep. Samāna, “equal”: friend and foe alike regard him without hostility (Śaṅkara).
m11: As A and U end in M when Om is said, waking and dream merge into deep sleep and come out of it again. “Measures”: he knows the world as it truly is (Śaṅkara).
m12: The Fourth is the silence after a-u-m. One who knows this, says Śaṅkara, is not born again.
